title: Unit final: the method
sub: Estimate from constraints, pick a collection, find the bug and the allocation, explain out loud
cards/0/q: The statement: 1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵, values up to 10⁹, a 1 second limit. What complexity do you aim for before you even know the idea?
cards/0/options/1: O(n²): the loops are simple, it will fit
cards/0/explain: n log n ≈ 2·10⁵ · 18 ≈ 3.6·10⁶ — far below 10⁸. n² = 4·10¹⁰ — 400 times over budget. So you look for sorting, a hash table, one or two passes, or a binary search.
cards/0/wrong/1: Simple loops win a few times over, but you are short by hundreds of times: 4·10¹⁰ versus 10⁸.
cards/0/wrong/2: Trying values up to 10⁹ for every element is 2·10¹⁴ operations. The value range is not a size you can iterate over.
cards/0/wrong/3: 2ⁿ works up to n ≈ 20, and here n is two hundred thousand.
cards/1/q: The limit is 1 second. Which solutions fit? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: n ≤ 15, trying all permutations in O(n!)
cards/1/options/1: n ≤ 22, trying all subsets in O(2ⁿ)
cards/1/explain: 2²² ≈ 4·10⁶, 2000² = 4·10⁶, 5000 · 5000 = 2.5·10⁷ — all under 10⁸. But 15! ≈ 1.3·10¹² — permutations only work up to n ≈ 10–11, and 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰.
cards/2/q: A matchmaking queue: take the player who has waited longest, and any player can leave the queue by id. Both operations must be O(1). What do you use?
cards/2/options/0: A LinkedList<Player> and a Dictionary<int, LinkedListNode<Player>> id → node
cards/2/options/2: A List<Player> with Add at the end and RemoveAt(0)
cards/2/options/3: A PriorityQueue<Player, float> by join time
cards/2/explain: The longest-waiting player is the head of the list, First, O(1). Leaving by id: the dictionary hands over the node, and Remove(node) is O(1). New players go in with AddLast, also O(1). The price is a node object per player, which is justified here.
cards/2/wrong/1: Taking the first is O(1), but you cannot remove a player from the middle of the queue except by rebuilding it, O(n).
cards/2/wrong/2: RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list — O(n), and leaving by id is a linear search, O(n) as well.
cards/2/wrong/3: Dequeue is O(log n), not O(1), removing by id is only possible by a scan (Remove in .NET 9 is O(n)), and Unity does not have this class.
cards/3/q: Update runs every frame, and units is a List<Unit>. One line creates heap garbage on every call. Tap it.
cards/3/explain: The lambda captures the local variable team: every Update call creates an object for the captured state and a new delegate. The for loop over a List<T> and the Vector3 arithmetic (a struct) produce no garbage. The fix is a loop instead of Exists, or team in a field and a delegate created once.
cards/4/task: Binary search for 66 in a sorted array of 12 elements. Step through the trace: the rig will stop twice and ask what the next check will be. Count how many comparisons it takes.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The candidates are [9..11]. What will the next check be?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 = 9 + 1 = 10: the middle of [9..11] is index 10, not 9. a[10] = 71 is greater than 66, so the answer is to the left, and the right part goes together with mid: hi = mid − 1 = 9.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: One candidate is left, [9..9]. What next?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The while (lo <= hi) loop also runs when lo == hi: mid = 9, a[9] = 66 — found. Four comparisons in total, where a left-to-right scan would have made 10.
cards/5/q: How many comparisons does a binary search make in the worst case on a sorted array of 10⁶ elements — and how many does a linear scan make?
cards/5/explain: Every comparison discards half of the candidates, and 10⁶ can be halved about 20 times: log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20. In the worst case a linear scan looks at all 10⁶ elements.
cards/5/wrong/1: 1000 is the square root of 10⁶. Binary search halves; it does not split into blocks of √n.
cards/5/wrong/2: n/2 is the average case of a linear scan. Binary search discards half at every step, so it takes log₂ n steps.
cards/5/wrong/3: Order does not help a linear scan: in the worst case it looks at all n elements.
cards/6/q: The function counts pairs i < j that sum to target; count maps a number to how many times it was seen. On [3, 3], target = 6 it returned 3, but there is one pair. Tap the line that is in the wrong place.
cards/6/explain: The invariant “the dictionary holds only elements to the left of the current one” is broken: x enters the counter before it looks for a partner, and with target = 2x it finds itself. On [3, 3] the first 3 pairs with itself (1), the second with both 3s (2), 3 in total instead of 1. Check first, insert after: the count[x] = c + 1 write has to move below the partner lookup.
cards/7/q: First Unique Character in a String (LeetCode #387): the index of the first character that occurs in the string exactly once. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: lowercase Latin only? What to return if there is none? How long is the string?
cards/7/items/2: Naive: for each character, recount it over the whole string — O(n²)
cards/7/items/3: Idea: the brute force counts the same letters again and again — count them all once in an int[26]
cards/7/items/4: Code: the first pass builds the counters, the second finds the first index with a count of 1
cards/7/items/5: Dry-run "loveleetcode": l and o occur twice, v once
cards/7/items/6: Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory for 26 counters; in Unity — stackalloc and zero allocations
cards/7/explain: The same seven-step script. The question “Latin only?” decides everything here: it determines whether an int[26] is enough or a dictionary is needed.
cards/8/q: Code from .NET 8 is being ported to Unity (C# 9, .NET Standard 2.1). What will not compile? Select all.
cards/8/explain: PriorityQueue arrived in .NET 6, the unsigned shift >>> in C# 11, collection expressions in C# 12. Span and stackalloc, HashCode and tuple keys are available in Unity: they are all part of .NET Standard 2.1 and C# 9.
cards/9/q: What is the complexity of this code?
cards/9/explain: Sorting is O(n log n), then n binary searches at O(log n) each — another O(n log n). The steps come one after another and add up: O(n log n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n).
cards/9/wrong/1: There is no second loop over the array inside the loop: BinarySearch is O(log n), not O(n).
cards/9/wrong/2: The logarithms would multiply if the binary search were nested inside the sort. Here the sort and the loop come one after another and add up.
cards/9/wrong/3: One pass is O(n), but every step does a log n binary search, and the sort itself costs n log n.
